Conditions for Patent Protection
How to test whether an invention may qualify for a patent.

THE BASIC IDEA
What is a patent?
A legal right for an invention.
It can stop others from making, using, or selling the invention without permission.
In return, the inventor explains how it works.

slides.title: CONDITION 01
suggestions: Break long sentences into shorter statements.
Check image quality, relevance, alignment, and attribution.
slides.extracted_text:
CONDITION 01
First condition: the invention must be new
The same solution must not already be available to the public.
Search
Patents, papers, products, and websites
Compare
Find what was already known or published
Identify prior art
Earlier knowledge that can affect protection
Test novelty
Ask whether the claimed invention is genuinely new
Prior art means earlier knowledge made available before the relevant filing date.

slides.title: CONDITION 02
suggestions: Shorten paragraphs and use concise bullet points.
slides.extracted_text:
CONDITION 02
Second condition: it must not be obvious
The invention must be a real step forward, not an easy next step.
The test
Would a skilled engineer reach this solution easily, using common knowledge?
Obvious
A fan with a motor is common. Adding a motor is an easy step.
Not obvious
A fan that cleans itself with a new mechanism is a bigger step, so it can be patented.
If the answer is yes, the idea is obvious and cannot be patented.

slides.title: CONDITION 03
findings: No issues detected by the basic automated checks.
suggestions: Check image quality, relevance, alignment, and attribution.
slides.extracted_text:
CONDITION 03
Third condition: it must be useful
The invention must work in practice, not only in theory.
Works
It performs the function it claims to perform.
Has a use
It has an industrial or business application.
More than theory
A purely theoretical idea is usually not enough.
Usefulness is often described as practical or industrial application. The exact legal test depends on the relevant law.

BEFORE YOU SEEK PROTECTION
Other checks before protection
Allowed subject
The subject must be allowed by the law.
Clear disclosure
The application must explain the invention clearly enough to reproduce it.
Correct office
File with the correct national or regional patent office.

Why choose a patent?
Protects a valuable technical solution.
Can support licensing, investment, and business advantage.
Useful when competitors could copy the product easily.

ANOTHER PATH
Why choose not to patent?
Cost and time
Patent applications take time and money.
Public disclosure
The invention becomes public through the application.
Trade secret
A confidential process may fit better when it is hard to discover.

A PRACTICAL FIRST PASS
A simple decision guide
Use these questions to decide what to investigate next.
Is it new? Search for prior art.
Is it a real technical improvement? Test the inventive step.
Can it be used in industry? Show a practical use.
Would public disclosure help more than secrecy? Compare disclosure and protection.
Ask a patent professional before filing.
This is a general overview. National laws differ, so check with the relevant patent office or a qualified patent professional.
